Intense physical stress, such as that in ultramarathon running, affects the immune system. For monitoring in sports medicine, non-invasive methods, e.g., salivary analysis, are of interest. This pilot cohort study aimed to assess changes in salivary parameters in response to an ultramarathon. The results were compared to blood parameters. Male, healthy finishers ( n = 9, mean age: 48 ± 8.8 years, mean height: 1.8 ± 0.1 m, mean weight: 72.5 ± 7.2 kg, mean BMI: 23.5 ± 1.9 kg/cm²) of a 160 km ultramarathon were included. Saliva and blood samples were collected at three time points: T1 (baseline), T2 (shortly after the ultramarathon) and T3 (after recovery). In saliva, cortisol, testosterone, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α, albumin, IgA, α-amylase, aMMP-8, and neopterin were assessed via ELISA. In blood, cortisol, testosterone, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α, blood cell counts, procalcitonin, CRP, osmolality, albumin, and α-amylase were analyzed. The statistical evaluation comprised longitudinal testing and cross-sectional testing between saliva and blood using ratios of T2 and T3 to baseline values. Various parameters in saliva and blood changed in response to the ultramarathon. Comparing blood and saliva, the longitudinal changes of testosterone ( p = 0.02) and α-amylase ( p = 0.03) differed significantly. Despite the limitations of the study, it underlines that saliva is an interesting option for comprehensive monitoring in sports medicine and necessitates further studies. endurance saliva immunoglobulin inflammation cytokines biomarkers University of Regensburg Department of Cariology, Endodontology and Periodontology, University of Leipzig Publication fees were supported by Open Access Publishing Fund of the University of Regensburg. Introduction Physical stress caused by intense exercise has various effects on the immune system [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]. Previous studies have monitored the effects of exercise on various blood parameters, including Interleukin (IL) IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10 and tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) [ 5 , 6 ]. These cytokines are inflammatory mediators of the immune system. The macrophage-derived mediator neopterin increases during training, too [ 7 ]. Furthermore, hormone levels change: cortisol increases and testosterone decreases [ 8 , 9 ]. However, blood sampling is an invasive method and requires medical expertise. Moreover, it can cause pain and stress. How to provide non-invasive monitoring of exercise is an ongoing question in sports medicine. One promising medium for this aim is saliva [ 10 ]. Saliva contains antibodies, growth factors, proteins, organic non-protein compounds, hormones, and specific salivary enzymes [ 10 ]. Fluctuations of the anabolic hormones cortisol and testosterone in saliva [ 3 ] and the correlation of these parameters measured in blood and saliva were reported [ 11 , 12 ]. Elevated levels of salivary IL-6 [ 13 ] and TNF-α [ 14 ] were observed. Studying parameters in saliva offers additional advantages. For salivary IgA, a decrease was observed in response to strenuous exercise and over a longer period of strenuous exercise, such as a football league season [ 15 ]. This could lead to reduced mucosal immunity and a higher incidence of infections [ 16 , 17 , 18 ]. Thus, its monitoring was discussed to prevent infections [ 16 , 17 , 18 ]. Salivary α-amylase increased in response to exercise [ 19 , 20 ] and could sensitively reflect psychophysiological stress [ 21 ]. Furthermore, salivary active matrix metalloproteinase-8 (aMMP-8) was examined because it is involved in extracellular breakdown and is used as a marker for periodontal degradation [ 22 ]. The present pilot study aimed to provide a comprehensive evaluation of changes in salivary parameters due to intense physical stress (ultramarathon), as well as relation of salivary parameters to simultaneous blood parameters. It was hypothesized that both blood and salivary parameters would differ significantly between baseline and after an ultramarathon or in the recovery phase. Additionally, it was hypothesized that there would be consistent changes in blood and saliva regarding the ratios of T2 (shortly after the ultramarathon) and T3 (after recovery) to baseline values.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Intense physical stress from ultramarathon running, encompassing exercise-induced responses, muscle damage, and physiological adaptation during load and recovery phases.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Intense physical stress significantly impacts the immune system and hormonal balance. Cortisol and testosterone changes are mediated by the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, with cortisol exerting immunosuppressive effects. Cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α) are key inflammatory mediators, while neopterin serves as a macrophage-derived mediator and a marker for oxidative stress. Adrenergic activity from psychophysiological stress activates salivary glands, increasing α-amylase concentrations. A decrease in IgA can compromise mucosal immunity, increasing infection risk. aMMP-8, an extracellular peptidase, is involved in tissue degradation. Creatine kinase indicates muscle damage, and urea levels are influenced by dietary protein intake.
related_biomarkers: Blood cell counts (including Erythrocytes, Leukocytes, Thrombocytes, Neutrophils, Lymphocytes, Monocytes, Eosinophils, Basophils)

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study focused on the physiological response to a single, intense 160 km ultramarathon, collecting samples at baseline (T1), post-race (T2), and after recovery (T3). Longitudinal analysis highlighted significant changes in many biomarkers from T1 to T2, with some returning towards baseline at T3. While no varying doses of ultramarathon were compared within this study, it was suggested that shorter distances could also influence s-cortisol and s-α-amylase with an intensity effect. Finisher status influenced s-IgA levels, which decreased for finishers but increased for non-finishers.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: Significant differences in longitudinal changes between salivary and blood compartments were found for testosterone (p = 0.02) and α-amylase (p = 0.03), suggesting distinct responses in these matrices. Specifically, the s-T2/T1 ratio for testosterone was 1.1 compared to 0.3 for blood, and for α-amylase, it was 67.8 for saliva versus 0.7 for blood. The association between salivary and blood values for testosterone appears less clear than for cortisol, for which T2/T1 ratios did not significantly differ between compartments. Different responses for serum and salivary IL-6 were reported, potentially indicating distinct origins. While no significant differences in pre- to post-exercise changes for IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 were identified between saliva and blood in this study, other research indicates such differences in high-intensity exercise. Creatine kinase is specific to recent muscle damage, and urea levels are highly sensitive to dietary protein intake.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The primary study population consisted of nine healthy, highly trained male ultramarathon runners (mean age 48 ± 8.8 years) who completed a 160 km ultramarathon within 30 hours, free from chronic diseases and permanent medication. The broader implications extend to athletes for load and recovery monitoring, individuals for biobehavioral stress assessment, and potentially patients with renal function issues, neurodegenerative diseases, and inflammatory bowel diseases.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Intense physical stress from ultramarathon running significantly impacts the immune system, causing acute physiological and immunological responses, including hormonal shifts, cytokine changes, and blood cell alterations. Monitoring these changes is crucial for understanding systemic stress, inflammatory impact, and for applications in sports medicine to manage athlete load and recovery, prevent overtraining syndrome, and minimize injury risk. Specifically, a reduction in salivary IgA (s-IgA) is linked to an increased risk of upper respiratory tract infections in athletes. While increased periodontal inflammation has been observed in elite athletes, s-aMMP-8 levels in this study did not indicate a threatening threshold. Saliva presents a promising non-invasive option for comprehensive monitoring, with blood parameters like cortisol, testosterone, IL-8, IL-6, and α-amylase also offering potential for innovative exercise and recovery tracking.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The findings highlight adverse risks such as reduced mucosal immunity, increased incidence of infections (especially linked to s-IgA reduction), overtraining syndrome, and potential injury risk. Conversely, there is significant diagnostic utility for monitoring exercise, recovery, and stress in athletes, and potential for diagnosing/monitoring various diseases. The comprehensive monitoring of load and recovery also offers a protective benefit against these adverse outcomes.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The pilot study, despite its small cohort (9 runners) and noted limitations, indicates saliva as a promising option for comprehensive monitoring in sports medicine. However, significant challenges in reliability were identified: high inter- and intra-individual variability (high SD) in both salivary and blood parameters, frequent measurements below detection limits for several biomarkers (e.g., s-IL-10, s-TNF-α, b-IL-1β, b-IL-6, b-IL-8), requiring cautious interpretation or correction. The relationship between salivary and plasma parameters is rarely investigated, and consistency between saliva and blood values is less clear for testosterone than for cortisol. Practical issues like reproducible saliva sampling, strict protocols, and consistent sampling time points are critical confounders. Other factors influencing results include oral health, collection methods, psychological conditions, BMI, age, body fat, pace, and storage conditions. Plasma creatine kinase and urea were deemed unreliable for general monitoring due to reflecting acute changes (muscle damage/dietary intake) and high variability, although salivary assessment is established for biobehavioral stress monitoring.
